patient.chief_complaint: Acute onset severe dizziness, nausea, difficulty swallowing, and unsteadiness
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Robert Halvorsen is a 58-year-old right-handed man with a history of hypertension and dyslipidemia who presents to the emergency department via EMS with acute onset severe vertigo, nausea, hoarseness, and difficulty swallowing beginning approximately 2 hours prior to arrival. The patient reports he was eating breakfast at home when he suddenly experienced intense room-spinning dizziness with nausea and one episode of vomiting. He stood up and immediately lurched to the right, grasping the counter. His wife noted he sounded hoarse and was coughing when trying to drink water. He also complained of a sharp, burning pain on the right side of his face. He called 911. There was no preceding headache, visual changes, limb weakness, or loss of consciousness. He denies any hearing loss or ear fullness. He did not notice numbness or weakness in his arms or legs, though his wife reports he appeared clumsy when trying to reach for his phone. Of note, he underwent chiropractic cervical manipulation approximately 36 hours prior for intermittent neck stiffness and soreness — a treatment he had received on two prior occasions without incident. On initial evaluation in the emergency department, the treating physician noted the patient's prominent dizziness and nausea, and initially considered a peripheral vestibular disorder such as vestibular neuritis or BPPV. A non-contrast CT head was ordered and reported as normal by radiology. However, the examining physician noted the crossed sensory findings on neurological examination — facial pain and temperature loss on the RIGHT and body pain and temperature loss on the LEFT — along with a right Horner syndrome, hoarseness, and right limb ataxia, which are inconsistent with a peripheral vestibular disorder. Neurology was urgently consulted. Time from symptom onset to ED presentation: approximately 2 hours. Last known well: 2 hours prior to arrival.

results.title: AHA/ASA 2019 Guidelines for Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke
results.authors: Powers WJ, Rabinstein AA, et al.
results.key_finding: IV alteplase is recommended within 3-4.5 hours of symptom onset for eligible patients. CT must precede thrombolysis to exclude hemorrhage. MRI DWI is more sensitive than CT for posterior fossa ischemia. CTA head/neck is indicated when LVO is suspected or vertebral dissection is considered.

results.title: HINTS Exam Outperforms Early MRI in Diagnosing Posterior Circulation Stroke in Acute Vestibular Syndrome
results.authors: Kattah JC, Talkad AV, Wang DZ, et al.
results.key_finding: The HINTS examination (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) had 100% sensitivity and 96% specificity for central cause of acute vestibular syndrome. A normal head impulse test, direction-changing nystagmus, or skew deviation each independently suggests a central (stroke) etiology.

results.title: Antiplatelet vs Anticoagulation for Cervical Artery Dissection (CADISS Trial)
results.authors: Markus HS, Levi C, King A, et al.
results.key_finding: No significant difference in stroke prevention outcomes between antiplatelet and anticoagulation therapy for cervical artery dissection. Recurrent stroke rate was low in both groups.

results.title: Wallenberg Syndrome: Clinical Features, Etiology, and Prognosis
results.key_finding: Lateral medullary infarction (Wallenberg syndrome) presents with crossed sensory loss, ipsilateral Horner, ipsilateral limb ataxia, ipsilateral dysphagia/dysphonia, and contralateral body pain/temperature loss. Vertebral artery disease is the most common etiology. MRI DWI is required for diagnosis; CT is frequently negative.

output.summary: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome is caused by infarction of the lateral medulla, most commonly from vertebral artery or PICA territory occlusion. The characteristic crossed sensory pattern (ipsilateral facial loss + contralateral body loss) and Horner syndrome localize the lesion to the lateral medulla. CT is frequently negative due to posterior fossa beam-hardening artifact; MRI DWI is the definitive imaging modality. For vertebral artery dissection, antiplatelet and anticoagulation therapy have shown equivalent outcomes in the CADISS trial; AHA/ASA 2019 guidelines recommend antithrombotic therapy for 3-6 months. The HINTS exam (negative head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew deviation) has high sensitivity and specificity for central vertigo and can guide urgent MRI ordering.

output.proposed: IV alteplase (tPA) 0.9 mg/kg for acute ischemic stroke, and/or antithrombotic therapy for vertebral artery dissection
interactions: Aspirin 81 mg daily: ongoing antiplatelet therapy is not a contraindication to IV alteplase, but increases baseline hemorrhagic risk; withhold additional antiplatelet/anticoagulant dosing for 24 hours after thrombolysis.
Atorvastatin: no clinically significant interaction with alteplase.
Lisinopril: no clinically significant interaction with alteplase; continue blood-pressure control targeting pre-tPA BP <185/110 mmHg.
contraindications: Vertebral artery dissection is not itself a contraindication to IV alteplase for the resulting ischemic stroke, when within the treatment window and other criteria are met (AHA/ASA 2019, Class IIa).
Intracranial extension of the dissection should be excluded before thrombolysis given subarachnoid hemorrhage risk; CTA in this case shows the dissection confined to the extracranial V3 segment.
warnings: Confirm INR <1.7, platelets >=100,000, glucose 50-400 mg/dL, and BP <185/110 mmHg before any thrombolysis decision.

For secondary antithrombotic therapy in vertebral artery dissection: antiplatelet (aspirin or clopidogrel) and anticoagulation (heparin/warfarin/DOAC) have equivalent efficacy per CADISS trial data; individualize choice.
Blood pressure management: do not aggressively lower BP in the acute phase before thrombolysis unless >185/110 mmHg.
output.formulary_status: IV alteplase on formulary for acute ischemic stroke; antiplatelet agents and anticoagulants on formulary
alternatives: If outside thrombolysis window or contraindicated: antithrombotic therapy for vertebral artery dissection — either antiplatelet or anticoagulation for 3-6 months per CADISS.
No proximal vascular occlusion identified on CTA, so mechanical thrombectomy is not applicable in this case.

critical_actions: Establish time of last known well (LKW) and apply NIHSS to determine acute treatment eligibility; this patient is within a 2-hour window
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision
Recognize the CROSSED sensory pattern (right facial + left body pain/temperature loss) as the hallmark of lateral medullary localization — do not attribute to peripheral vestibular disorder
Perform HINTS exam: negative head impulse test, direction-changing nystagmus, and skew deviation identify central vestibular syndrome and mandate urgent MRI DWI
Do NOT rely on normal CT to exclude posterior fossa ischemia — MRI DWI is required when CT is negative and clinical suspicion persists
Obtain CTA neck to evaluate right vertebral artery dissection as the stroke mechanism, prompted by recent chiropractic manipulation
Assess tPA eligibility within the 4.5-hour window; vertebral artery dissection is not itself a contraindication to thrombolysis
Initiate antithrombotic therapy (antiplatelet or anticoagulation) for vertebral artery dissection per CADISS evidence for 3-6 months
Initiate continuous telemetry and cardiac monitoring; begin secondary prevention workup including echocardiogram
Monitor for bulbar deterioration (aspiration risk from dysphagia), cerebellar edema, and obstructive hydrocephalus — neurosurgical consultation if mass effect develops
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose peripheral vestibular neuritis or BPPV and discharge — crossed sensory findings, Horner syndrome, and dysphagia exclude a peripheral vestibular etiology
Do not rely on a normal CT scan to exclude posterior fossa ischemic stroke — CT is frequently negative due to beam-hardening artifact in the posterior fossa; MRI DWI is the definitive modality
Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not give IV tPA if INR >1.7, platelet count <100,000, or other guideline-listed contraindications are present
Do not aggressively lower blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg in the acute phase outside the tPA window — risks worsening brainstem perfusion
Do not delay vessel imaging in posterior circulation stroke — vertebral artery dissection must be characterized urgently to guide antithrombotic therapy
key_reasoning_points: Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome produces a pathognomonic crossed sensory pattern: IPSILATERAL face pain/temperature loss (spinal trigeminal nucleus) + CONTRALATERAL body/limb pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic tract) — uniquely localizing to the lateral medulla

Additional ipsilateral signs of Wallenberg syndrome — Horner syndrome (sympathetic fibers), limb ataxia (inferior cerebellar peduncle), dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), and vertigo — all ipsilateral to the infarcted lateral medulla
Critically, corticospinal tracts are SPARED in the lateral medulla: NO limb weakness is the key discriminator from pontine or more extensive brainstem strokes

CT is frequently NEGATIVE for posterior fossa ischemia due to beam-hardening artifact at the skull base; a normal CT does NOT exclude brainstem or cerebellar infarction — MRI DWI is mandatory when clinical suspicion exists

The HINTS bedside exam (negative/normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew deviation) has sensitivity and specificity exceeding early MRI for identifying central causes of acute vestibular syndrome

Right vertebral artery dissection following chiropractic cervical manipulation is the most likely mechanism; fat-saturated T1 MRI demonstrating intramural hematoma is the diagnostic hallmark of cervical arterial dissection
For vertebral artery dissection-related stroke, antiplatelet and anticoagulation therapies have equivalent outcomes (CADISS trial); AHA/ASA 2019 recommends antithrombotic therapy for 3-6 months
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Non-contrast CT is the required first-line study in the acute window; MRI adds tissue-based selection and is not mandatory for the diagnosis.

AHA/ASA 2026 sequencing: glucose is checked before thrombolysis, but routine CBC/coagulation results are not awaited without a reason to expect abnormality; ECG/troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA/CTP do not wait for creatinine.

red_herrings.data_point: Normal non-contrast CT head reported by radiology
red_herrings.intended_effect: A naive agent anchoring on the normal CT may conclude no acute intracranial pathology and consider peripheral vestibular disorder, missing the posterior fossa ischemia that is beyond CT resolution
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: CT is insensitive for posterior fossa ischemia due to beam-hardening artifact; a normal CT in a patient with crossed sensory signs, Horner syndrome, and dysphagia mandates urgent MRI DWI, not discharge

red_herrings.data_point: Prominent vertigo, nausea, and vomiting at presentation
red_herrings.intended_effect: Vertigo and nausea as the leading symptoms may anchor an agent toward peripheral vestibular etiology (BPPV, vestibular neuritis), particularly when CT is normal — the most common misdiagnosis of Wallenberg syndrome in the ED
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The combination of vertigo with crossed sensory findings, ipsilateral Horner syndrome, dysphagia, and ipsilateral ataxia localizes definitively to the central nervous system (lateral medulla); peripheral vestibular disorders do not cause these features
